pages.title: Speech errors II · The positional level and beyond
From a message to articulated speech
pages.c: A **speech-production model** separates choosing a message from organizing and pronouncing it. At the functional level, the speaker selects word meanings and assigns semantic roles. At the positional level, those choices enter a grammatical structure. Phonological encoding specifies the sound sequence, and speech gestures turn that sequence into movements of the articulators.
support: A speech error can preserve one kind of organization while disrupting another. A sentence may keep its grammatical frame even when the wrong word enters it. A different error can keep the intended words but exchange their sounds. These patterns give us evidence about the representations used during production.
pages.d: The important distinction is between the information a stage organizes and the observable speech that eventually comes out. Lemmas, noun phrases and phonemes are theoretical units whose usefulness comes from explaining patterns across errors. An error that leaves grammatical structure intact while changing its occupants is informative because the two components behave differently.
pages.visual: The model runs from a conceptual message through functional and positional organization to phonological encoding and speech gestures. The lowest box concerns articulation. The boxes above it organize meanings, grammatical roles and sound plans rather than movements themselves.

pages.title: Semantic roles and positional structure
pages.c: In “Where’d I bring it when I put it in?”, the **functional level** supplies two verb lemmas, BRING and PUT, together with their participants. The speaker, expressed as I or ME, is the agent of both actions. IT is the undergoer of both. This information identifies the events and who participates in them, but a grammatical sentence also has to express how the events are related.
support: The positional level organizes that information into clauses and grammatical positions. The relationship between the actions, the question structure and the forms required by tense all contribute to the eventual sentence. Knowing which participant performs an action is therefore different from knowing where each word belongs in the spoken sequence.
pages.d: Think of the functional representation as identifying two actions with the same agent and undergoer. The positional representation has the additional job of arranging those actions in an English sentence. The distinction helps explain how a speaker can preserve the intended participants while putting a verb into the wrong grammatical location.
pages.visual: BRING and PUT name the selected verb lemmas. I/ME and IT identify participant roles across both events. These role assignments do not themselves specify the final order or the verb forms demanded by the question and the embedded clause.

pages.title: Grammatical slots determine verb forms
pages.c: The question frame “Where’d I [verb, root form] it when I [verb, past] it in?” contains two different verb requirements. The first clause includes the auxiliary did, so its main verb takes the base form. The clause introduced by when requires a past-tense form. The **positional level** supplies those grammatical requirements as well as positions for the selected lemmas.
support: If BRING and PUT enter the wrong positions, their forms can still fit the positions they occupy. This separates the identity of the selected lemma from the inflection required by the sentence frame. The frame also contains grammatical material such as the auxiliary and the organization needed for a wh-question.
pages.d: A word-order error does not have to destroy the grammar around it. A lemma can enter an unintended slot and still receive the form that slot requires. That is why the difference between a root-form slot and a past-tense slot matters when diagnosing the error.
pages.visual: The brackets identify grammatical requirements rather than spoken words. The first bracket calls for a base verb after did. The second calls for a past form. Those different requirements remain meaningful even if the two selected verb lemmas exchange positions.

pages.title: Analyzing “a language needer learns”
pages.c: The error “a language needer learns” can be analyzed against the intended pattern “a language learner needs.” LEARN and NEED have exchanged the positions where their roots would ordinarily appear. The **agent-noun ending -er** remains with the noun position, while the third-person singular ending -s remains with the finite verb position.
support: The resulting expression still has a noun phrase followed by a verb. Its unusual form needer is particularly useful because it combines NEED with an ending normally attached to LEARN in this expression. This makes the error evidence about how roots and affixes are assembled rather than just which familiar word is retrieved.
pages.d: To analyze the error, keep the moving material separate from the grammatical material that stays in place. LEARN and NEED move. The noun-forming -er and the verb ending -s continue to mark their original positions. The result reveals an organization below the level of a whole stored word.
pages.visual: Compare learner with needer and needs with learns. Each pair preserves an ending while changing its root. That paired comparison is the basis for calling the affixes stranded in their grammatical positions.

pages.title: Stranded derivational and inflectional affixes
pages.c: In “a language needer learns,” two lemmas exchange positions while the positional structure stays largely intact. The noun is formed from a verb root plus the **derivational affix -er**. The final verb receives third-person singular -s. The error therefore preserves two different kinds of morphology even as the roots fill unintended positions.
support: Derivational morphology can change the kind of word being formed. Adding -er to a verb creates an agent noun, as in learner. Inflectional morphology expresses a grammatical requirement on the word, as the singular verb ending does in learns. Both affixes remain interpretable in the error.
pages.d: This is more specific than a claim that two complete words were swapped. A complete swap of learner and needs would carry their endings with them. Instead, the roots change places and the endings stay attached to the grammatical jobs represented by the noun and verb positions.
pages.visual: The tree separates the noun phrase, NP, from the verb phrase, VP. Inside the noun phrase, the noun position is represented as a verb plus -er. The verb position separately specifies third-person singular morphology. Those positions explain why needer and learns emerge.

pages.title: Analyzing “He did that easy enoughly”
pages.c: The error “He did that easy enoughly” places the **adverb-forming ending -ly** on enough rather than easy. The intended expression “easily enough” attaches -ly to easy. The produced sequence preserves the suffix but combines it with a different root, giving the unusual form enoughly.
support: This example invites two related questions. One concerns the attachment of the affix to its root. The other concerns the grammatical arrangement that puts easy and enough in their positions. Both questions matter because the error changes the relation between the words as well as the word carrying the ending.
pages.d: The useful comparison is between easily enough and easy enoughly. The suffix remains available for building an adverb, but it is applied to the wrong item. A successful explanation has to account for that attachment and for the arrangement of the two roots.
pages.visual: The written contrast makes the stranded -ly visible. Easy loses the ending that would normally produce easily, while enough receives it. Keeping these intended and produced forms distinct prevents the error from being reduced to a vague claim about mispronunciation.

pages.title: An error in arranging the positional frame
pages.c: “Easy enoughly” and “a language needer learns” both contain a **stranded affix**. In the first example, -ly is the derivational ending that can turn an adjective into an adverb. However, the analysis of easy enoughly also involves a change in how the positional structure is set up, rather than simply exchanging two lemmas inside an otherwise unchanged frame.
support: The two trees contrast an arrangement with an adverb followed by an adjective against one with an adjective followed by an adverb. The -ly ending is associated with the adverb position. Changing which root occupies that position produces the unusual enoughly while leaving easy without its expected ending.
pages.d: The shared feature across the examples is the separation of roots from affixes. Their difference is the behavior of the frame. The needer example preserves its basic noun-and-verb organization. The easy enoughly example changes the organization represented by the two adjective-phrase trees.
pages.visual: AP labels the larger phrase. Adv and Adj distinguish the adverb and adjective positions, and Adj plus -ly specifies how the adverb is built. The lower starred structure puts the adverb position after the adjective position, connecting the structural change to the produced error.

pages.title: Errors provide evidence for productive morphology
pages.c: Novel forms such as needer and enoughly suggest that word production can combine roots with **separately represented affixes**. If every derived form were retrieved only as a complete stored word, related words such as need, needy and needless could be linked in the lexicon without requiring a separate suffix representation. Producing a new combination on the fly provides a different kind of evidence.
support: The error analysis supports three connected ideas. Lemmas and affixes are represented separately in some way. Affixes have positions in the grammatical organization of an utterance. A grammatical process can generate a derived word, including a form that is unusual in the intended expression.
pages.d: The key observation is productive recombination. The speaker does not merely replace one familiar derived word with another. A root appears with an affix that belongs to a different position in the planned expression. That pattern gives a concrete reason to include morphological operations in a production model.
pages.visual: The linked sets need–needy–needless and learn–learner–unlearn illustrate a whole-word alternative. Needer and enoughly supply the contrasting evidence because their formation is explained by combining roots and affixes during production.

pages.title: Morphology also changes the sound form
pages.c: A grammatical instruction to add an affix leaves **phonological work** to be completed. Easy becomes easily, and the error enoughly applies -ly to enough. More complex derivations such as certificate, certification and recertification change the sound pattern of the base as well as adding material. Vowels and stress can change as part of forming the derived word.
support: The positional level can specify a morphological operation such as making an adjective into an adverb. Phonological encoding then supplies the sequence and organization of sounds appropriate to the resulting form. The morphological plan and its pronunciation are related stages of the process rather than identical representations.
pages.d: Affixation is more than attaching an unchanged spoken fragment to an unchanged base. The certificate family illustrates why a model needs a way to translate a morphological structure into its correct pronunciation. Stress marks and vowel differences identify aspects of that translation.
pages.visual: The transcriptions contrast easy with easily and enough with enoughly, followed by the certificate word family. The changing stress marks and vowel symbols make the central point visible. Related morphological forms can require different phonological patterns.

pages.title: Phonological encoding orders phonemes
pages.c: **Phonological encoding** turns selected lemmas, affixes and grammatical particles into a sequence of phonemes. “Easy enoughly” contains an unusual morphological combination, but its sound sequence can still be well formed. By contrast, fish grotto becoming gish frotto and “with this ring I do wed” becoming “with this wing I do red” involve changes in the arrangement of speech sounds.
support: Chomsky and Halle becoming Chomsky and Challe is another sound-level example. Menn describes such errors as neat because the resulting sequences follow English phonotactic patterns and can be articulated clearly. A phonological planning error can therefore produce a crisp, recognizable sound sequence even when the sequence is unintended.
pages.d: An error in the planned phoneme string differs from an error in carrying out the articulatory movements. In phonological encoding, an unintended sound can occupy a well-defined position and then be pronounced normally. The structure of the error concerns which phonemes were selected or ordered.
pages.visual: Fish/gish and grotto/frotto exchange initial consonants. Ring/wing and wed/red similarly redistribute sounds across words. Comparing the intended and produced pairs identifies what moved while showing that the surrounding word structure remains recognizable.

pages.title: Speech gestures execute the sound plan
pages.c: The **speech-gestural level** converts a planned sequence of phonemes into motor actions. Errors in these actions can produce imprecise or unclear speech. This differs from a neatly produced phonological error, where the sound plan itself contains an unintended sequence but the movements execute that sequence successfully.
support: The change from ad hoc to odd hack illustrates an ambiguity taught by the model. The two vowels could have exchanged at the phonological-encoding level. A change in tongue positioning during execution could also produce the observed contrast. The intended and produced sound patterns therefore have to be interpreted in relation to articulatory detail.
pages.d: The distinction is between selecting a different vowel category in the plan and executing a different tongue position. Both routes can change the vowels a listener hears. The model separates these mechanisms even when an informal report of an error does not uniquely identify which mechanism occurred.
pages.visual: The vowel chart locates vowels by tongue height and front–back position. Ad hoc and odd hack redistribute the low-vowel qualities associated with their syllables. The spatial organization of the chart connects that acoustic contrast to the tongue-position account.

pages.title: Separating morphological and sound-level errors
pages.c: The collected examples involve different kinds of change. Buyed contrasts with the irregular past form bought, making it a **morphological regularization**. Arising becoming arriving changes a consonant within a closely similar word form. Pronouncing close as [kloʊz] in “pretty close to here” changes the final consonant from the voiceless form expected for the adjective.
support: Throfly for thoroughly changes several aspects of the sound sequence, so its analysis starts by comparing the actual intended and produced sounds. Each example should be located by the kind of representation that changed, such as a past-tense form, a selected word form, or the sequence used in pronunciation.
pages.d: Keep morphology separate from phonological resemblance. Buyed has a recognizable regular past-tense pattern applied to a verb with an irregular past. The close example instead concerns a phonemic distinction in a particular lexical use. Grouping both as simply a wrong word would hide the different processes involved.
pages.visual: The production model supplies the levels against which the examples can be compared. Buyed/bought directs attention to word formation, while the explicit [kloʊz] transcription directs attention to the final voiced consonant. The arrows distinguish intended forms from reported productions.

pages.title: Comparing errors across representational levels
pages.c: “Wash my teeth and brush my face” exchanges verbs while leaving their arguments in place. “Following vowel” becoming “vollowing fowel” **exchanges initial consonants**. Seat heaters becoming heat seaters also moves sound material while leaving the plural ending with seaters. These contrasts distinguish the movement of lexical roots from the movement of individual sounds.
support: Lana del Rey becoming Marina del Rey introduces a related familiar name sequence. “For all intensive purposes” replaces part of a familiar expression with a different word sequence. The interrupted speech-language pathology production preserves attempts and repairs, which are useful parts of the observed behavior rather than a single finished substitute.
pages.d: The informative question is what remains organized while another component changes. In the teeth/face example, the clause structure and object positions remain. In following/vowel, the recognizable surrounding sound sequences remain while their initial consonants exchange. These are different patterns that a multilevel production model can distinguish.
pages.visual: The quoted examples contain both completed errors and an interrupted production. The sequence “speech plath... speech plang” contains successive attempts and a repair. Treating it as a single clean word replacement would discard part of the evidence.

pages.title: Interpreting “a hundred-dollar room” in context
pages.c: The expression “you enter a hundred-dollar room and you do yoga” occurred in a discussion of hot yoga. The context matters because the amount could concern the temperature of a room rather than its price. The word dollar is a meaningful word in an unexpected relation to the intended description.
support: This example directs attention to the relationship between the message and the selected lexical material. The clause remains grammatical and the words are pronounceable. The unusual part is the meaning contributed by dollar in the hot-yoga context, so an account must explain selection in relation to the intended event.
pages.d: The same spoken phrase can be ordinary in one situation and an error in another. A hundred-dollar room is sensible in a discussion of cost. Hot yoga supplies the contextual information that makes the reported wording worth examining as a production error.
pages.visual: The quoted utterance supplies the produced wording, and the note “re hot yoga” supplies the relevant context. The production diagram distinguishes choosing a concept and a lemma from organizing phonemes and articulation. The example chiefly invites examination of the former choices.

pages.title: Interpreting “Law and Order SUV”
pages.c: “Law and Order SUV” substitutes the familiar letter sequence SUV for the title sequence SVU. The same three letters are present, but their order changes. This makes the example useful for distinguishing the organization of a form from the concepts and associations that may make a competing form available.
support: SVU belongs to the program title, while SUV is a familiar vehicle abbreviation. Comparing those two forms identifies the rearrangement precisely. The familiarity of the produced sequence also makes it relevant to ask whether an existing competing form was selected rather than assuming that every reordering is an isolated motor slip.
pages.d: The observable pattern is an exchange in the final two positions of the abbreviation. A production analysis should begin with that pattern and then consider which representations contain the two familiar sequences. The utterance remains easy to articulate despite its mismatch with the intended title.
pages.visual: The vehicle image makes the meaning of SUV salient, while the program reference supplies the intended context. These associations explain why the competing abbreviation is recognizable. The meaningful contrast is SVU versus SUV, not simply the presence of an unusual word.

pages.title: Interpreting chicken becoming kitchen
pages.c: “He cooked his kitchen” replaces the intended chicken with kitchen. The two words share much of their sound structure, and their initial and medial consonants occur in opposite positions. They also both have a meaningful relationship to cooking. The error therefore brings sound similarity and the semantic context together.
support: The intended object is chicken, while the produced object is kitchen. Both fit the noun position after his, so the sentence retains its grammatical frame. The comparison should therefore focus on the selection and organization of the word form rather than a failure to create a grammatical object position.
pages.d: The example illustrates why a production analysis starts with both the actual forms and the context. A consonant-order comparison captures the relation between chicken and kitchen, while the cooking context explains why kitchen is a meaningful competitor. These are different properties of the same reported error.
pages.visual: Chicken and kitchen exchange the positions associated with their initial and medial consonants while retaining a similar syllabic pattern. The sentence and parenthetical intended word identify the direction of the substitution.

pages.title: Observation depends on attention and context
pages.c: Collecting spontaneous speech errors depends on **what an observer notices and records**. Expectations about a production model can direct attention toward particular kinds of errors. Learning to recognize exchanges, substitutions or stranded affixes can change which events stand out and how they are described.
support: Interpreting an error also requires reconstructing the intended message and the situation in which it occurred. A form can be grammatical and meaningful in isolation yet inappropriate for the speaker’s intention. Context therefore contributes evidence about what changed, while the observer’s expectations can influence which analysis seems most immediate.
pages.d: An observed collection is produced through a sequence of decisions. Someone notices a sound, treats it as an error, remembers its wording and chooses a description. Studying those decisions helps explain why spontaneous-error records are not a neutral sample of every production event.
pages.visual: The questions distinguish what an observer listened for, what was heard, what was reported and what contextual information was used. Those are separate steps in building and interpreting the evidence.

pages.title: Perception shapes reported speech errors
pages.c: **Speech perception** can shape the errors that observers record. Listeners are not especially good at hearing sounds halfway between phoneme categories, particularly consonants. They also tend to perceive phonotactically legal sequences and familiar words. An ambiguous sound between giss and kiss can therefore be heard more like kiss.
support: These tendencies can make some production errors less noticeable than others. A listener may report a clean phoneme substitution even when the articulation was intermediate, or perceive an unfamiliar sequence as a familiar word. Theory-dependent observation also includes the influence of the observer’s expectations on the description of the event.
pages.d: Experimental methods add control over what is presented and how responses are measured. This helps separate the produced signal from the perceptual and reporting processes that shape an informal error record. The methodological issue follows from particular properties of speech perception, not from a general claim that observation is useless.
pages.visual: The giss/kiss contrast makes lexical familiarity relevant to an ambiguous signal. The other two examples concern category boundaries and legal sound sequences. Together they explain why the distribution of reported errors can differ from the distribution of produced events.

questions.stem: Why can exchanged verb lemmas still appear in grammatically appropriate forms?
choices: Positional slots specify the forms required by their grammatical roles.
The motor system independently reconstructs the sentence meaning.
The speaker retrieves every clause as an indivisible stored unit.
The phoneme sequence determines semantic roles before word selection.
questions.why: A base-form slot and a past-tense slot impose different requirements even when unintended lemmas occupy them.

questions.stem: What makes “a language needer learns” evidence about morphological assembly?
choices: The roots exchange while -er and -s remain with their grammatical positions.
The noun phrase disappears and is replaced by a second verb phrase.
Both whole words exchange together with their original endings.
The articulators produce vowels between two categories.
questions.why: Needer combines NEED with the noun-forming ending, while learns combines LEARN with the finite-verb ending.

questions.stem: How does “easy enoughly” differ from the needer example in the proposed analysis?
choices: Its analysis includes a change in the positional organization as well as a stranded affix.
It contains no separately identifiable affix.
It can only arise during articulatory execution.
It preserves two entire stored words without recombination.
questions.why: The adjective-phrase trees change the order of adjective and adverb positions, with -ly belonging to the adverb position.

questions.stem: Why are novel forms such as enoughly theoretically useful?
choices: They indicate that roots and affixes can be combined productively during production.
They prove that no complete derived words are ever stored.
They show that grammatical structure is absent from speech planning.
They establish that listeners perceive every error accurately.
questions.why: The source uses new root–affix combinations as evidence for separately represented components and a grammatical process of derivation.

questions.stem: Why does adding a derivational affix leave work for phonological encoding?
choices: The derived form can require changes in vowels and stress as well as added material.
Affixes always preserve every sound and stress position of the base.
Derivation determines only the intended speaker and listener.
Phonological encoding decides whether the event is in the past.
questions.why: The certificate family illustrates changes in sound pattern associated with derivation.

questions.stem: A speaker clearly says gish frotto instead of fish grotto. Which property supports a phonological-encoding analysis?
choices: The initial consonants are rearranged into clearly produced, phonotactically possible sequences.
The intended participants have exchanged semantic roles.
The final consonants are too imprecise to identify.
The phrase has lost every recognizable sound from the intended words.
questions.why: The error concerns which phonemes occupy positions in an otherwise neatly executed sound plan.

questions.stem: Why does ad hoc becoming odd hack not uniquely identify one production level?
choices: It can reflect a vowel exchange in the phonological plan or altered tongue positioning during execution.
Both forms contain no vowels.
The two forms differ only in their spelling.
The positional level has no relationship to grammatical form.
questions.why: The model distinguishes phoneme planning from articulatory execution even when an informal observation could fit either mechanism.

questions.stem: Why is buyed in place of bought especially informative about morphology?
choices: It applies a recognizable regular past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
It exchanges the agent and undergoer of an event.
It removes the distinction between consonants and vowels.
It shows that the verb has no grammatical tense.
questions.why: The error is organized around the form expressing past tense, rather than merely an unclear articulation.

questions.stem: Why does the situation surrounding a spontaneous error matter?
choices: It helps identify what the speaker intended and how the produced wording departed from that intention.
It guarantees that the error originated at the motor level.
It eliminates the influence of perceptual expectations.
It allows the observer to ignore the exact produced wording.
questions.why: The same phrase can be appropriate in one context and erroneous in another, as illustrated by the hot-yoga example.

questions.stem: How can perception bias a collection of spontaneous speech errors?
choices: Ambiguous or unfamiliar sequences may be heard as familiar words or legal phoneme sequences.
Listeners reliably hear every intermediate consonant as intermediate.
Word familiarity affects only spelling and cannot affect perception.
All errors are equally likely to be noticed regardless of expectations.
questions.why: Categorical, phonotactic and lexical perceptual biases can make reported errors differ from the events that were produced.

written.prompt: Explain what “a language needer learns” reveals about roots, affixes and positional structure.
answer: Compare it with a language learner needs. LEARN and NEED exchange positions while the endings remain associated with their grammatical jobs.
The noun position combines a verb root with derivational -er, and the verb position supplies third-person singular -s. This supports separable roots, affixes and positional organization.

written.prompt: Distinguish phonological-encoding errors from speech-gestural errors, using a supplied example for each issue.
answer: Phonological encoding specifies the phoneme sequence. Fish grotto becoming gish frotto is a neatly articulated exchange in that sequence.
Speech gestures execute the articulatory movements and can produce imprecise speech. Ad hoc becoming odd hack is ambiguous because it could involve vowel planning or tongue positioning.
